Wi-Fi Captive Portal

Wi-Fi Captive Portal: Deep Technical Analysis

Oct 23, 2026

Overview

A captive portal is a Layer-3 gateway policy, not a Wi-Fi feature. The client associates and gets an address normally, and a stateful enforcement point blocks forwarding until a web or API transaction marks that client as authorized. Nothing in IEEE 802.11 defines it. The IETF standardizes only discovery (RFC 8910) and a status API (RFC 8908), plus an informational architecture (RFC 8952). Everything else interception, the login UI, the session model and the firewall mechanics is implementation specific.

Typical Deployments
DeploymentTypical access method
Public hotspots and cafésTerms-of-service click-through
HotelsRoom number + surname, or PMS-issued voucher
AirportsTime-limited free tier, paid upgrade
Enterprise guest accessSponsor approval, SMS/email OTP
Subscription hotspotsAccount login, often RADIUS-backed
Home routersGuest SSID with a simple portal

Component Roles

ComponentRole in the portal
Wireless client (STA)Associates, runs DHCP/SLAAC, runs OS captive-portal detection, renders the login page.
AP / hostapd + driverBeacons, association, keying, per-STA isolation (ap_isolate), VLAN tagging; emits STA connect/disconnect events. No HTTP role.
DHCP server (dnsmasq/odhcpd)Assigns addresses, advertises RFC 8910 option; leases are the main IP↔MAC binding source.
DNS resolverResolves walled-garden names; must answer truthfully.
Gateway / firewallThe enforcement device: drops or redirects unauthorized forwarding, NATs authorized traffic.
Portal web serverServes the splash page, the RFC 8908 API and the login endpoint.
Portal controller / session DBMaps client → session, holds state, programs the firewall, handles expiry.
Authentication backend / RADIUSValidates credentials or vouchers; returns policy (session timeout, bandwidth, VLAN); receives accounting.

End-to-end Connection Flow

The client reaches the Internet only after thirteen hand-offs, and only stages 10–11 are portal-specific; most field failures happen at stages 4–7, before any login.

Captive Portal Detection on Client Devices

Every major OS uses two mechanisms:

  • positive signal (RFC 8910 option → RFC 8908 API)
  • legacy cleartext HTTP probe to a vendor host whose exact response it knows

Any deviation a redirect, a different body, an empty 200 is read as “captive”, a timeout or reset is read as “no Internet”, which shows no login prompt. Probe URLs below are as documented by the vendor where a vendor document exists; anything marked observed comes from third-party captures and can change without notice.

Standards-based Discovery

  • The network places an HTTPS API URI in DHCPv4 option 114, DHCPv6 option 103 or IPv6 RA option 37. RFC 8910 replaced RFC 7710, whose DHCPv4 code 160 conflicted with other uses (RFC 8910). The URI urn:ietf:params:capport:unrestricted tells clients they can skip detection.
  • The client sends GET with Accept: application/captive+json; the server must answer with that content type and a JSON body whose only mandatory key is captive (boolean). Optional keys: user-portal-url, venue-info-url, can-extend-session, seconds-remaining, bytes-remaining (RFC 8908).
  • The API must be HTTPS with a certificate valid for the provisioned hostname; if validation fails the client must ignore the API and fall back to legacy behaviour. Responses should carry Cache-Control: private or no-store. A captive network should still allow OCSP/CRL and NTP so the client can validate the certificate.
  • Client identity: if the API server cannot see the client’s identity itself (e.g. the API is off-box and NATed), RFC 8908 §4 recommends a per-client API URI (e.g. /captive-portal/api/X54PD39JV) handed out in each DHCP lease.

System Architecture

The gateway is the only place that sees all guest traffic, has the DHCP bindings, and can NAT. The APs only bridge the guest SSID into VLAN 30 and isolate clients; they hold no authorization state, so roaming between them does not affect the portal session.

Comparison of Deployment Models

Gateway-based enforcement with an optionally external or cloud-hosted portal UI is the right default for embedded products; AP-based enforcement only makes sense for standalone single-AP devices or with a controller that synchronizes state.

AspectA. Gateway-basedB. AP-basedC. Centralized enterprise (controller)D. External portalE. Cloud-managed
Traffic flowAP bridges to gateway; gateway redirects, enforces, NATsAP filters/redirects locally (often bridge-family rules), then bridges or routesAPs tunnel (CAPWAP/GRE/VXLAN) or VLAN-trunk guest traffic to controller/anchorEnforcement local; splash/login on a remote web server, result returned to enforcement point via signed redirect or APILocal enforcement (AP or gateway) driven by cloud policy; portal often cloud-hosted
Session-state locationGatewayEach APController (replicated in HA pairs)Enforcement point + external serverCloud DB, cached on device
RoamingTransparent across APs on the same L2 guest VLANLost on roam unless APs sync stateTransparent (central anchor)Same as the enforcement point usedDepends on whether device or cloud is authoritative; usually re-auth by MAC on new AP
ScalabilityHundreds to low thousands of clients per gateway (CPU/conntrack bound)Scales with APs, but per-AP RAM is smallHigh, controller-sizedPortal scales independentlyHigh; enforcement still local
Security boundaryOne hardened box; guest never touches AP managementEvery AP is an enforcement point and must be hardenedStrong; guests tunneled away from local LANMust authenticate the callback (HMAC/token), or anyone can grant accessCloud account and device-cloud channel become attack surface
External dependencyNone for local ToS/voucherNoneController reachabilityLogin impossible if WAN or portal host is downLogin and policy changes depend on WAN + cloud; define offline behaviour
Operational complexityLow–mediumLow per box, high at scaleHighMediumLow for operator, high for vendor
Home routerBest fitAcceptable (single AP)OverkillRareCommon in ISP CPE
HospitalityGood (PMS integration on portal server)WeakGood for large hotelsCommon (vendor portal)Very common
Public hotspotGoodWeakGood (carrier)CommonVery common
Enterprise guestGood for branchesWeakBest fitCommon (sponsor portal)Common
ModelTypical useKey strengthMain limitation / design note
Gateway-basedSingle-site routers and gatewaysSees every packet, owns DHCP bindings, applies IPv4 and IPv6 policy consistentlyCPU for TLS and nftables set size on small SoCs; budget conntrack entries per client
AP-basedStandalone APs that also route (travel routers, single-AP SOHO)No separate gateway neededWith multiple bridged APs, each sees only its own clients, so a roam re-captures the client unless the session is pushed to all APs. Bridge-family filtering needs br_netfilter or the nftables bridge family and must handle IPv6 ND and DHCP explicitly
Centralized controllerLarge enterprise and campusGuest traffic tunneled to an anchor controller (often in a DMZ): strong isolation, one session storeTunnel MTU overhead; dependency on the controller
External portalVendor or hosted login UI (openNDS calls it FAS; vendors call it external captive portal)UI and authentication scale independently of the enforcement boxSecurity rests on the token exchange: the enforcement device redirects with a signed query string, the external server calls back with a token. openNDS, for example, sends a hashed client id and requires a return hash computed with a pre-shared faskey (openNDS FAS)
Cloud-managedMulti-site operatorsSame as D, plus central configuration and reportingDefine WAN-loss behaviour: fail-closed (no new logins), fail-open for existing sessions, or a local ToS fallback

Captive Portal on OpenWrt with uspot + spotfilter

ScopeDesign, porting and hardening of a production captive portal for OpenWrt-based access points, built on uspot (control plane) and spotfilter (eBPF data plane)
AudienceFirmware / platform engineers, portal & RADIUS backend engineers, QA
Baseline codeuspot (OpenWiFi, J. Crispin) and spotfilter (F. Fietkau) as provided in uspot.zip and spotfilter.zip
Target platformQualcomm-based OpenWrt AP (fw4/nftables, NSS ECM present)
StatusDraft for development — sections marked [VERIFY] must be confirmed on target hardware

Why is the uspot

ConcernCoovaChilli (current)uspot + spotfilter (target)
Client data pathEvery client packet passes through the chilli process (raw socket → tun0)Kernel forwarding; packets never enter userspace
ThroughputBounded by one userspace process on the AP CPUBounded by kernel / hardware forwarding
DHCP for clientsChilli’s own DHCP serverStandard OpenWrt dnsmasq
Access decisionPer packet in userspaceeBPF classifier sets a firewall mark; fw4 enforces
fw4 / nftables integrationIndirect (iptables-nft shims, duplicate-packet RST issue required an extra prerouting rule)Native: one mark, a handful of fw4 rules
Accounting countersChillieBPF per-client counters
Code baseC, largely unmaintained (v1.6 on target)ucode + small C/eBPF components, part of the OpenWrt/OpenWiFi ecosystem
